questions.do: Type Mariner 4 in the Search names and descriptions box and read its card.
questions.a: Launched on 28 November 1964, it made the first successful Mars flyby and took the first close-up image of another planet. Its picture is in Seen by the spacecraft as "First TV Image of Mars".

questions.q: Which Indian mission in the archive carries an "A first" badge, and what was the first?
questions.do: In the nation menu, pick India. Read the cards and look for the A first badge. You can also press Firsts only.
questions.a: India shows 5 missions. Chandrayaan-3 (launched 14 July 2023) has the badge: the first soft landing near the lunar South Pole. Chandrayaan-1 discovered water on the Moon, but its line does not use the word "first", so it gets no badge.

questions.q: Which years had the most launches in the archive?
questions.do: On the Launches by year chart, find the tallest columns of dots. Click near 1965 and read the note under the chart. Then click near 1967.
questions.a: 1965 and 1967 each show 12 missions, the most of any year. Many of the dots in those columns are grey Moon missions.

questions.q: Mariner 10 is famous for the first Mercury flyby. Why does it appear under the Moon filter?
questions.do: Click the Moon filter and search Mariner 10. Read its description. Then read the footer about how destinations are sorted.
questions.a: Its line begins "Lunar and Venus flybys in addition to the First Mercury flyby". The footer says destinations are sorted automatically from names and descriptions, so a few may be misfiled. The Moon rule is checked first and the word "Lunar" matches, so it lands under Moon.

questions.q: In 1959, which mission first reached the Moon's surface, and which first photographed its far side?
questions.do: Press Firsts only, then search Luna (or click the 1959 column on the timeline). Read the cards.
questions.a: Luna 2 (12 September 1959) was the first artificial object on the Moon, by impact. Luna 3 (4 October 1959) took the first images of the far side of the Moon. Both were Soviet, launched two years after Sputnik 1 (4 October 1957).
